context.hint: A Go authorization service issues HMAC-signed session tokens. Password login rejects a disabled account, but the token parser checks only account existence, optional stored token-identifier membership, and password modification time. A local test already showed that a disabled account's validly signed token with an intact identifier is accepted by a fresh settings view, while an enabled control and a project-role token pass. The next question is where to place the smallest enabled-state check so account tokens are rejected without changing project-role tokens, identifier revocation, password-time invalidation, or enabled sessions.
context.surface: A Go authorization service with a session manager, an account and project settings store, a token parser with separate account and project-role branches, server authentication middleware, and package-level tests backed by fake settings clients.
assumptions: The observer can read and modify a disposable local source tree, run the local Go toolchain, and create fake settings clients; no public target, production service, or installed dependency is used.
The attacker holds an existing validly signed token for an account that is later disabled and cannot change the server signing key.
An enabled account token and a project-role token are legitimate controls that must keep working.
Stored token-identifier removal and password modification time are existing revocation mechanisms that must keep working after the repair.
Official benchmark evaluation is host-side; local package tests and a clean patch application are not an official pass.

incumbent.text: Hypothesis: the token parser trusts stored token-identifier membership and skips live enabled state, so a disabled account with an intact identifier still authenticates. Prerequisites: two local accounts sharing a signing key, one enabled control with a stored identifier, and one account disabled after issuance with its identifier retained. Bounded test: issue both tokens, switch only the disabled account flag in a fresh settings view, replay both through the public parser, then re-enable and replay again. Expected supporting result: the disabled token is rejected while the enabled token and the post-re-enable token are accepted. Falsifier: the disabled token is accepted or the enabled control is rejected. Cleanup: restore the flag and discard the fake clients.

candidates.text: Hypothesis: inserting the enabled-state check immediately after account lookup and before identifier membership rejects disabled accounts without altering revocation logic. Prerequisites: the vulnerable local source, fake settings clients, one disabled account with a valid identifier, and one enabled account with a revoked identifier. Bounded test: apply the minimal check, replay the disabled valid-identifier token, the enabled token, and the revoked-identifier token, and compare error classes. Expected supporting result: the disabled token fails with a disabled error, the enabled token succeeds, and the revoked token still fails for a missing identifier. Falsifier: any disabled token succeeds or a control changes its error class. Cleanup: restore fixtures and retain the patch in a disposable copy.

Hypothesis: placing the enabled check after password-modification-time validation also rejects a disabled account but lets the time error mask the disabled state. Prerequisites: a token issued before both a password change and a disablement. Bounded test: create that token, change the password time, disable the account, and replay against a fresh view; compare the error with a disabled-only control. Expected supporting result: rejection occurs, but the error is time-specific unless enabled state is checked first. Falsifier: the token is accepted or a disabled-only token is accepted. Cleanup: restore the original password hash and account flag.

Hypothesis: a project-role token remains valid after an associated account is disabled because its validation branch is independent of account state. Prerequisites: a project role with a stored role identifier and an account whose enabled flag can change. Bounded test: issue a role token, disable the associated account, and replay the role token through the parser without changing project settings. Expected supporting result: the role token succeeds, showing orthogonality. Falsifier: the role token fails with an account-state error. Cleanup: restore the account and project fixtures. Limitation: the role subject is not a local account, so this is a branch-isolation regression rather than an account-token behavior.

Hypothesis: the server authentication middleware propagates a parser error for a disabled account instead of falling back to an anonymous identity. Prerequisites: a local server fixture with anonymous fallback configured and a validly signed disabled-account token. Bounded test: present the token through the middleware token slot and inspect the returned context subject and status code; repeat with an enabled token. Expected supporting result: the disabled token yields an unauthenticated error and the enabled token yields the correct subject. Falsifier: the disabled token yields an anonymous successful context. Cleanup: close the server fixture.

Hypothesis: concurrent enable and disable toggles do not create intermittent acceptance because the parser reads a copied account view rather than shared mutable state. Prerequisites: a settings fixture whose enabled flag can be toggled while tokens are parsed. Bounded test: toggle the flag in a loop while parsing the same token in parallel workers, recording every verdict and panic. Expected supporting result: each parse reflects either the enabled or disabled state consistently, with no panic. Falsifier: a parse accepts after disablement or crashes. Cleanup: stop workers and restore the final flag.

evaluations.rationale: The incumbent has direct local evidence: a disabled account with an intact identifier parsed successfully while enabled and project-role controls passed. It remains the baseline to repair but does not specify patch placement or error-order regression, so it is deferred.

Selected. It gives the minimal placement in the account branch and a matrix that separates disabled-state rejection from identifier revocation. The earlier observation supplies the vulnerable baseline, so one action can test the repair and lifecycle controls.

Deferred and folded into the selected regression matrix. Checking after password-time validation also rejects the token, but the error becomes time-specific. The same matrix can include a changed-password control without choosing this placement.
Deferred, not refuted. The earlier test already showed a project-role token accepted independently, so the expected result is supported before the repair. It is retained as a post-repair regression.

Deferred, not refuted. Middleware propagation is a real downstream boundary, but the server fixture is larger than the package-level repair check and the parser already returns an error. It is a plausible later robustness check.

Deferred, not refuted. Concurrent toggling is a distinct concern, but the parser receives account copies and the new predicate adds no shared mutable state. Lower value than patch application and lifecycle regression.

observation.summary: Applied the minimal enabled-state predicate after account lookup and before identifier membership. A validly signed token issued for the account while it was enabled now failed with an unauthenticated disabled-account error. Controls passed: an enabled account token was accepted, a project-role token remained accepted, a missing identifier still failed with a token-identifier error, a later password time still failed with a password-change error, and disabled state took precedence over a changed password. The complete session package test suite passed in the development tree. A one-hunk patch was saved. Local only; no official evaluation ran.
observation.next_hint: Apply only the saved one-hunk patch to a pristine copy and reproduce the disabled rejection with the full control matrix.
